slot.brief: Monatomic gas heat added at constant volume; find temperature rise using first law

stem: A sample of $2\text{ mol}$ of an ideal monatomic gas is kept inside a rigid container. If $498\text{ J}$ of heat is supplied to the gas, the rise in its temperature is: (Take $R = 8.3\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$)

verdicts.working: Rigid container ⇒ constant volume, W=0, Q = nCvΔT with Cv = 3R/2 = 12.45 J/mol·K. ΔT = 498/(2×12.45) = 20 K.

working:
For a rigid container, the volume remains constant, so the work done by the gas is zero ($W = 0$).

By the First Law of Thermodynamics:
$$Q = \Delta U + W = \Delta U$$

For an ideal monatomic gas, the molar heat capacity at constant volume is:
$$C_v = \dfrac{3}{2}R$$

The change in internal energy is given by:
$$\Delta U = n C_v \Delta T$$

Therefore:
$$Q = n \left(\dfrac{3}{2}Right) \Delta T$$

Substituting the given values:
$$498 = 2 	imes \left(\dfrac{3}{2} 	imes 8.3ight) 	imes \Delta T$$
$$498 = 3 	imes 8.3 	imes \Delta T = 24.9 \, \Delta T$$
$$\Delta T = \dfrac{498}{24.9} = 20	ext{ K}$$

Independent check: Rigid container ⇒ constant volume, W=0, Q = nCvΔT with Cv = 3R/2 = 12.45 J/mol·K. ΔT = 498/(2×12.45) = 20 K.

draft.distractor_notes:
Option A ($10\text{ K}$) comes from omitting the factor of $1/2$ in the formula for $C_v$ (using $C_v = 3R$) or inadvertently doubling the number of moles.
Option B ($12\text{ K}$) comes from mistakenly using the molar heat capacity at constant pressure $C_p = \dfrac{5}{2}R$ instead of $C_v = \dfrac{3}{2}R$.
Option D ($40\text{ K}$) comes from neglecting the number of moles ($n = 2$) and calculating with $n = 1$.
